question.problem:
Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $5$ datapoints with $3$ features in the form of the $5\times 3$ matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-0.6 & -0.95 & -1.02 \\ 0.79 & 0.33 & 1.56 \\ -1.48 & -1.17 & -0.66 \\ 0.67 & 0.8 & -0.15 \\ 0.63 & 0.99 & 0.27\end{aligned}]
$$

where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$).
We are also given the SVD decomposition $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ where:

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.462 & 0.174 & -0.685 & 0.1 & 0.527 \\ 0.473 & -0.718 & -0.24 & 0.358 & 0.272 \\ -0.613 & -0.29 & 0.546 & 0.457 & 0.181 \\ 0.253 & 0.517 & -0.053 & 0.798 & -0.17 \\ 0.35 & 0.319 & 0.416 & -0.127 & 0.766\end{aligned}] \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}3.171 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.32 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.477 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.615 & 0.231 & -0.754 \\ 0.587 & 0.505 & 0.633 \\ 0.527 & -0.832 & 0.175\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. 

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components.

We should pick components based on 
{{field-1}}.

If we wish to preserve $95%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=3.171,\,{\sigma }_{2}=1.32,\,{\sigma }_{3}=0.477.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.171}^{2}}{{3.171}^{2}+{1.32}^{2}+{0.477}^{2}}≈83.6%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.171}^{2}+{1.32}^{2}}{{3.171}^{2}+{1.32}^{2}+{0.477}^{2}}≈98.1%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $83.6%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $98.1%$ of the variance.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14225071/assets/1d967881aaa7c2a7cd7f537d70d3637edae36b3edf62e15ac67949925d5ee2ef.png)

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions},$ since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $95%$ of the variance.
